analysis.one_liner: Tightens the ban on unwanted robocalls and forces phone companies to verify callers' identities.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 429-3 with 237 bipartisan cosponsors in July 2019, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Federal Communications Commission to write rules clarifying that automated calls and texts need your consent, lets you withdraw that consent, and makes callers keep records proving they had it. It requires phone companies to adopt caller-verification technology at no extra charge to customers, makes it easier to fine repeat illegal robocallers and refer them to the Justice Department, sets up protections against one-ring phone scams, and creates a panel to shield hospitals from robocall flooding.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone. The bill would force callers using automated dialers to prove they had consent, let consumers revoke consent, and require phone companies to verify that caller ID is real so scammers can't fake a local number. It would also make opt-out call-blocking free, add up to $10,000 to fines for intentional violations, and send evidence of fraudulent robocall operations to the Justice Department for prosecution.

how_it_helps.text: The FCC must write rules ensuring automated calls and texts are made only with consent, that consumers can withdraw that consent, and that callers keep records proving they obtained it.
Phone companies must implement call-authentication technology that verifies a caller's number is real, and may not charge consumers or small businesses an added line-item fee for it.

The FCC can impose forfeiture penalties on illegal robocallers without first issuing a citation when violations were intentional, gains a three- or four-year window to pursue them, and can add up to $10,000 to the penalty for intentional violations.

The FCC must share evidence of willful, repeated, fraudulent robocall violations with the Attorney General, and the Justice Department must convene an interagency working group on robocall enforcement, including whether to increase criminal fines and prison terms.

The FCC must open a proceeding to protect people from one-ring scams, in which a brief call prompts the victim to call back and be charged; the bill also creates the Hospital Robocall Protection Group to combat robocalls targeting hospitals.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that profit from high-volume automated calling — telemarketers, collection agencies, and outright scammers — would face tighter rules, bigger fines, and more referrals for prosecution. Phone and internet-calling providers bear the cost of installing caller-verification technology and tracing infrastructure, though they are barred from billing consumers for it through line-item charges.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban robocalls; it leaves exemptions in place for categories like government, debt collection, and healthcare calls, simply requiring the FCC to attach limits on who may call whom and how often under those exemptions — so exempted robocalls would continue.

Enforcement depends on the FCC and the Justice Department actually acting: several provisions are studies, reports, and proceedings rather than immediate rules, and large portions of the bill give the Commission discretion on timing and scope.

Small and rural phone providers may be exempted from the six-month implementation deadline if they show technical burdens, meaning some calls in those networks could go unverified longer; the bill requires the FCC to develop alternative protections without extra customer charges during any exemption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefits to phone users are large and the costs to the public are essentially none, since carriers are forbidden from passing implementation costs to customers through line-item fees. The main honest criticism is design rather than direction: the bill leans heavily on FCC rulemaking, studies, and advisory groups rather than outright bans, and leaves exemption channels open for debt collectors and other callers, so results would depend on how aggressively regulators enforced the new tools.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 429-3 in July 2019 and sent it to the Senate, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 20, 2019, with bipartisan sponsorship: 237 cosponsors, including 170 of 231 House Democrats and 67 of 197 House Republicans.
The Energy and Commerce Committee advanced the amended bill on July 17, 2019, by a 48-0 vote and reported it the next week.

On July 24, 2019, the House passed the bill under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority — by 429-3, with every voting Democrat in favor and 195 of 197 Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill on July 25, 2019, and no further action was ever taken on it; it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of illegal robocall and spoofing operations came out ahead, since the tools to fine and prosecute them never took effect. Phone carriers also avoided the mandates the bill would have imposed, and the exemption channels for high-volume callers stayed as they were.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: on final passage, 234 of 234 voting Democrats and 195 of 197 Republicans voted yes, with 3 Republicans voting no.

industries.note: The bill requires consent records, tightens exemption limits, raises penalties up to $10,000 for intentional violations, and channels evidence of fraud to the Justice Department. Its cost falls directly on businesses that profit from mass automated calling.

industries.industry: Robocall scam operators and caller-ID spoofers
industries.note: Caller-authentication mandates, one-ring scam proceedings, easier forfeitures without prior citations, and DOJ referrals target precisely the practices that generate scam losses for ordinary phone users.

Carriers and internet-calling providers would bear the cost of implementing call-authentication technology and tracing coordination, but the bill shields them by barring extra line-item charges to consumers, exempting small and rural providers with technical burdens, and embedding them as the permanent channel for call tracing and blocking services.

The bill requires the FCC to ensure opt-out robocall-blocking services are free to consumers with transparency and redress for wrongly blocked calls — growing demand for blocking while capping what providers can charge.
